concepts.summary: Many traditions picture the sky as a male elder: a remote, all-seeing father whose rain makes the earth fertile and whose authority stands behind kings and oaths. The clearest case is linguistic. Vedic Dyauṣ Pitā, Greek Zeus Patēr and Latin Iuppiter all descend from a reconstructed Proto-Indo-European *Dyēus ph₂tēr, 'Sky Father'. Outside that family the resemblance is looser and probably independent: the sky is simply the largest, highest, least reachable thing there is. Several peoples even tell how this father withdrew from daily life, and Egypt reverses the genders entirely.

versions.title: Nut Arched Over Geb
versions.teaser: Egypt flips the pattern: the sky is a mother, the earth a father.
versions.text:
In Egypt the sky is a woman. Nut stretches over the world on fingertips and toes, her star-spangled belly forming the vault of heaven, while her brother-husband Geb, the earth, lies beneath her, sometimes propped on one elbow. Between them stands their father Shu, the air, holding them apart so that there is room for life to happen.

Nut is also a mother in the most literal cosmic sense. Each evening she swallows the sun and each dawn she gives birth to it again; tomb ceilings show the solar disc travelling through her body. The dead hoped to join her as stars. The Pyramid Texts address her as the one who takes the king into her arms.

So the Egyptian 'sky father' is no father at all, a useful reminder that the Indo-European pattern is one habit of thought, not a law of nature.
sources: The Book of Nut (cenotaph of Seti I, Abydos)

image.caption: Shu holds the sky goddess Nut above the reclining earth god Geb; Greenfield Papyrus, c. 940 BCE, British Museum

versions.title: An, the Distant Heaven
versions.teaser: The oldest god of heaven, so exalted that he hardly ever acts.
versions.text:
The Sumerian word an means 'sky', and An is the sky as a god: first in the god lists, father of the great gods, the source of kingship, which was said to have 'descended from heaven'. His city was Uruk, whose great temple, the Eanna, 'House of Heaven', bore his name, though it belonged chiefly to Inanna.

Yet An is strikingly passive. In the opening lines of the Sumerian poem of Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld, heaven and earth are parted, 'An carried off heaven, Enlil carried off earth', and thereafter it is Enlil and Enki who do the work of running the world. In the Babylonian Enūma Eliš, Anu is sent against Tiamat, looks at her, and turns back.

He is the model of a sky god who has authority rather than energy, respected by everyone and consulted by the younger gods mainly for his signature.

versions.title: Dyaus and Pṛthivī
versions.teaser: Heaven the father and Earth the mother, praised always as a pair.
versions.text:
In the Rigveda the sky god Dyaus is almost never alone. He appears in the dual compound Dyāvāpṛthivī, 'Heaven-and-Earth', a single divine couple invoked as the wide, unaging parents of gods and men. Whole hymns are addressed to them together, asking the two to be kind, like a father and mother to their children.

The poet of Rigveda 1.164 says plainly: 'Dyaus is my father, my begetter; the navel is here; my mother is this great Earth.' His name and epithet, Dyauṣ Pitā, match Greek Zeus Patēr and Latin Iuppiter sound for sound, which is why historical linguists treat him as the direct heir of an inherited sky father.

But in Vedic practice he has faded. Indra, Agni and Soma receive the hymns and the offerings; Dyaus survives as a grand old name, honoured and scarcely used.

versions.title: Tian and the Son of Heaven
versions.teaser: Heaven grants the right to rule, and takes it back from tyrants.
versions.text:
For the Zhou dynasty, who overthrew the Shang around 1046 BCE, the highest power was Tian, 'Heaven'. Tian was less a person with adventures than a watchful moral authority above the world. It conferred the Mandate of Heaven (tianming) on a virtuous ruler and withdrew it from a cruel one. The Zhou used exactly this argument to justify their conquest: the last Shang king had lost Heaven's favour by his vices.

The ruler therefore bore the title Tianzi, 'Son of Heaven', and only he could make the great sacrifice to Heaven. In the Book of Documents and the Book of Odes Heaven sees and hears through the people, and 'Heaven's mandate is not constant'.

Centuries later the Ming emperors still walked out each winter solstice to the round altar in southern Beijing to report to their father.
versions.caveat: Tian is often impersonal and moral rather than paternal; 'father' applies mainly through the royal title 'Son of Heaven'.

versions.title: Zeus, Father of Gods and Men
versions.teaser: The cloud-gatherer who rules Olympus is everyone's father, at least by title.
versions.text:
Homer calls Zeus again and again 'father of men and gods', patēr andrōn te theōn te, and 'cloud-gatherer'. He sends rain and lightning, sits on the highest peak, weighs the fates of heroes on golden scales, and guards the laws of hospitality and oaths. His name comes from the same root as Vedic Dyaus; Zeus Patēr is Dyauṣ Pitā in Greek dress.

Unlike his Vedic cousin, Zeus did not fade. Hesiod's Theogony makes him the youngest son of Kronos, who defeats his father and the Titans and then rules by dividing honours fairly among the gods. The title 'father' is often political rather than biological: he is father as a king is father of his people.

Though, given his record in the genealogies, the biological sense is also frequently accurate.

image.caption: The 'Zeus of Otricoli', Roman marble copy of a 4th-century BCE Greek original, Vatican Museums

versions.title: Ukko, the Old Man Above
versions.teaser: The Finnish 'Old Man' of the sky, called on for rain and thunder.
versions.text:
Ukko means simply 'old man', and in Finnish and Karelian runo-song he is the god of the upper air: 'Ukko, the highest god, the old man of the heavens', who holds up the sky, drives the clouds and makes thunder. Singers call on him in charms when they need rain for crops or strength against a sickness.

The earliest written notice is hostile. In 1551 the Lutheran reformer Mikael Agricola listed the gods of the Tavastians in the preface to his Finnish psalter, noting that Ukko brought rain and thunder and that people held drinking feasts, Ukon vakat, in his honour at spring sowing.

In Lönnrot's Kalevala Ukko is the court of last appeal: when the heroes are stuck, they pray to the old man in the sky, and he usually answers.
sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
versions.caveat: The Kalevala is Lönnrot's 19th-century compilation from folk songs, so its framing is partly his own.

versions.title: Ranginui Pushed Away
versions.teaser: Sky and Earth embraced so tightly their children lived in darkness.
versions.text:
In the beginning Ranginui, the Sky Father, lay pressed upon Papatūānuku, the Earth Mother, and their many sons were cramped in the darkness between them. The brothers debated what to do. Tūmatauenga, the fierce one, wanted to kill their parents; Tāne Mahuta, lord of forests, proposed only to separate them.

One by one the brothers tried and failed, until Tāne lay on his back, planted his head on his mother and his feet against his father, and slowly pushed Rangi up into the heavens. Light flooded the world. Only Tāwhirimātea, the winds, took his father's side and has made war on his brothers ever since.

Rangi still grieves. His tears fall as rain and dew on Papa, and the mist that rises from her valleys is her answering sigh.

versions.title: Nyame and the Pestle
versions.teaser: The sky god once lived close to earth, until a pestle struck him.
versions.text:
The Akan high god Onyankopɔn Nyame is the sky. Asante tell that long ago he lived just above people's heads, so near that they could touch him. An old woman pounding fufu kept hitting him with the upper end of her long pestle, and at last Nyame, offended, moved far up to where he is now.

The old woman told her children to pile up every mortar they could find to climb to him. The tower almost reached; they needed one more. 'Take the bottom one and put it on top,' she said. They did, and the whole stack came down.

Nyame did not vanish from religion. Asante compounds once kept a forked post, Nyame dua, 'God's tree', holding a pot for offerings to the sky. But he is the classic 'withdrawn god' of African religion: supreme, and at a courteous distance.

image.caption: An Asante Nyame dua shrine (right), holding rainwater for the sky god, beside a Jamaican Revival shrine

concepts.summary: The earth as mother is one of the most natural metaphors in religion: she bears crops, receives the dead, and is often the partner of the sky. Yet her character varies widely. She may be a nurturing 'mother of all', a stern guardian of moral law, or a devouring monster who must be fed. The Indo-European pairing of sky father and earth mother is partly inherited, but most earth mothers arise independently from agricultural life. Scholars now distrust the older idea, popularised by Marija Gimbutas, of a single prehistoric Great Goddess behind them all.

versions.title: The Hymn to the Earth
versions.teaser: 'Earth is my mother, I am her son': a Vedic poet's vow.
versions.text:
The twelfth book of the Atharvaveda opens with a long hymn, the Pṛthivī Sūkta, addressed entirely to Bhūmi, the Earth. It praises her mountains, rivers and forests, the fragrance that rises from her, the peoples of many languages and customs she carries 'as a cow gives milk'.

Its most famous line is the twelfth verse: mātā bhūmiḥ putro ahaṃ pṛthivyāḥ, 'Earth is my mother, I am the son of Earth.' The poet asks forgiveness in advance for digging into her: 'What I dig from you, O Earth, may that quickly grow again; may I not strike your vitals or your heart.'

It is one of the earliest texts anywhere to treat the land with something like ecological courtesy, and modern Indian environmental writing quotes it constantly.

versions.title: Gaia, Mother of All
versions.teaser: Earth comes first, gives birth to Sky, and plots against him.
versions.text:
In Hesiod's Theogony, after Chaos comes 'broad-breasted Gaia, the ever-secure seat of all'. Without any partner she gives birth to Ouranos, the starry Sky, 'equal to herself, to cover her on every side', and then bears him the Titans, the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers.

Gaia is not merely passive soil. When Ouranos pushes his children back into her body, she groans under the weight, forges a great sickle of adamant, and hands it to her youngest son Kronos to cut down his father. Later she advises Zeus how to win his own war, and afterwards bears Typhon to challenge him. Earth, in Greek myth, always takes the long view.

The Homeric Hymn to Earth greets her more gently, as 'mother of all, oldest of all', who feeds everything that walks, swims or flies.
sources: Homeric Hymn 30, To Earth Mother of All

image.file: File:Feuerbach Gaea.jpg
image.caption: Gaea, ceiling painting by Anselm Feuerbach, 1875, Academy of Fine Arts Vienna

versions.title: Jörð, Mother of Thor
versions.teaser: The Norse earth, of giant stock, is the mother of the thunder god.
versions.text:
Norse myth personifies the earth as Jörð, whose name is simply the common word for 'earth'. Snorri Sturluson calls her Odin's daughter and also his wife, and makes her the mother of Thor. The poets knew this well: in Lokasenna and elsewhere Thor is addressed as Jarðar burr, 'son of Earth'.

She is otherwise a quiet figure, with no surviving myth of her own; Snorri counts her among the goddesses while elsewhere implying that she was of giant stock. Her importance is genealogical. The strongest god, defender of Midgard, is the child of the sky's ruler and the ground itself.

The pairing is instructive. The thunderstorm that splits the heavens is, in this family tree, the earth's own son come home.
versions.caveat: Jörð has almost no narrative of her own; she is known mainly from genealogies and poetic kennings.

versions.title: The Earth That Weeps at Night
versions.teaser: The earth feeds everyone, but at night she cries out to be fed.
versions.text:
Not every earth mother is gentle. The sixteenth-century Histoyre du Mechique, a French translation of a lost Spanish account of Nahua traditions, calls the earth a goddess, Tlaltecuhtli: a monster with biting mouths at every joint, whom Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca tore in two to make the world (her dismemberment is told under "A World Made from a Slain Giant").

What follows makes her a mother. The other gods, pitying her, decreed that everything people need to live would come from her body: trees, flowers and herbs from her hair, grass from her skin, springs and small caves from her eyes, rivers and great caves from her mouth, valleys and mountains from her nose and shoulders.

But her fruitfulness has a price. At night, the text says, she weeps, craving human hearts, and will not be quiet until she is given them; nor will she bear fruit unless she is watered with human blood.

Her carved image was often placed face down, meant to be seen by the earth, not by people.
versions.caveat: The Histoyre survives only in a French translation of a lost Spanish account, and Tlaltecuhtli's gender varies in the sources.

image.file: File:Tlaltecuhtli monolith.jpg
image.caption: The Tlaltecuhtli monolith, found at the Templo Mayor, Mexico City, in 2006

versions.title: Pachamama Must Drink First
versions.teaser: Before anyone drinks, a few drops go to the thirsty Earth.
versions.text:
In the Andes the earth is Pachamama, 'Mother of the World' or 'Mother of Time and Space', since pacha covers both. She is the living ground that gives potatoes and maize and the pasture for llamas, and she is owed a return. Spanish priests of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, hunting 'idolatries', complained that farmers offered her chicha, coca and llama fat before ploughing and at harvest.

The custom never stopped. At a meal or a fiesta in Peru or Bolivia today, people still spill a little drink on the ground before drinking, the ch'alla, saying it is for Pachamama. August, the dry month before planting, is when she is hungriest and receives buried offerings.

Colonial painters absorbed her too: the famous Virgin of the Mountain of Potosí shows Mary's robe as the silver mountain itself.
versions.caveat: Colonial descriptions were written by hostile missionaries, and modern Pachamama devotion is deeply blended with Catholic Marian piety.

versions.title: Papatūānuku, the Land Below
versions.teaser: The Māori earth mother holds the living and receives the dead.
versions.text:
After her husband Ranginui was pushed into the sky, Papatūānuku remained below as the land itself, the mother from whom every tree, bird and person descends. Her children dwell on her body; the forests are her garments, the mist rising from her valleys her grief for the husband far above.

In one strand of the tradition, when Tāne needed a wife, he went first to his mother, and she told him to form a woman from the earth at Kurawaka. So humanity itself is shaped from her soil.

The relationship is written into the Māori language. Whenua means both 'land' and 'placenta', and the old custom is to bury a newborn's placenta in ancestral ground, returning it to Papa. Tangata whenua, 'people of the land', is how Māori describe themselves as the country's first inhabitants.

versions.title: Moist Mother Earth
versions.teaser: Russian peasants swore oaths on a clod of damp earth.
versions.text:
In Russian folk speech the earth is Mat' syra zemlya, 'Moist Mother Earth'. Nineteenth-century folklorists recorded that peasants treated her as a living person with rights. Oaths were sworn by taking a clod of earth and placing it on one's head or swallowing it; boundary disputes were settled by a man walking the line with turf on his head. In some villages the earth was not to be struck or dug on certain holy days, because 'the earth is pregnant' in spring.

People in trouble could confess their sins to the ground itself, kneeling and speaking into a hole. In the spiritual verses of wandering singers, the earth weeps over human wickedness and begs God to let her be cleansed.

Whatever she was before Christianity, by the time she was written down she had become a devout, long-suffering mother among the saints.
versions.caveat: Attested only in Christian-era folk practice; claims about a pre-Christian earth goddess behind it are reconstruction.

versions.title: Ala, Keeper of the Law
versions.teaser: The Igbo earth goddess judges crimes as offences against the land.
versions.text:
Among the Igbo of southeastern Nigeria, Ala (also Ani or Ana) is the earth, the most important deity in daily life. She gives fertility to fields and families and receives the dead into her body, but above all she is the guardian of custom. Serious wrongs such as murder, incest or theft of yams are nso ala, 'abominations against the earth', and must be ritually cleansed or the whole community suffers.

In the Owerri area, communities built mbari houses in her honour: open shrines filled with painted clay sculptures of Ala, her children, animals, market women, even colonial officers, built over months by specially chosen people and then left to crumble back into the earth.

Readers of Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart meet her as Ani, whose Week of Peace Okonkwo disastrously breaks.
sources: Herbert M. Cole, Mbari: Art and Life among the Owerri Igbo (1982)

image.file: File:Urata-Igbo Mbari house dedicated to Amadioha, photographed by William Fagg near Owerri. British Museum.jpg
image.caption: An Igbo mbari house near Owerri (this one dedicated to Amadioha), photographed by William Fagg; British Museum

concepts.summary: Across the ancient Near East and the Indo-European world, a god of storm and thunder fights a great serpent or water monster, and his victory releases rain, secures kingship, or holds back chaos. The resemblances between the Vedic, Hittite, Canaanite, Greek and Norse versions are close enough that scholars such as Calvert Watkins argued for an inherited formula, 'the hero slew the serpent', while others stress diffusion across the Near East. Similar serpent-slayings from Japan remind us that the pattern can arise independently wherever storms, rivers and snakes seem like forces to be tamed.

versions.title: The Storm God and Illuyanka
versions.teaser: Beaten once, the storm god returns with a feast and a trap.
versions.text:
The Hittite text recited at the spring purulli festival tells two versions of one story. In the first, the serpent Illuyanka defeats the Storm God. The goddess Inara prepares a feast, with vessels of wine and beer, and enlists a mortal, Hupašiya, who asks to sleep with her as his price. The serpent and his children come up from their hole, drink until they are too bloated to go back down, and Hupašiya ties them with a rope. The Storm God comes and kills them.

In the second version Illuyanka has taken the Storm God's heart and eyes. The god fathers a son who marries the serpent's daughter and asks for them as his bride-price. Restored, the Storm God goes out to fight, and when his son takes the serpent's side, he kills them both.

It is, pointedly, a victory of cunning before it is one of strength.

image.file: File:Anatolian Civilizations Museum slaying of the serpent Illuyanka by the Storm God in 2011 02.jpg
image.caption: Storm gods attacking the serpent, relief from the Lion Gate at Arslantepe (Malatya), Museum of Anatolian Civilizations

versions.title: Indra Slays Vṛtra
versions.teaser: The serpent held back the waters until Indra split him open.
versions.text:
'I will proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra,' begins Rigveda 1.32: 'he slew the serpent, released the waters, and split the bellies of the mountains.' The serpent is Vṛtra, 'the Obstruction', who lies coiled on the mountains holding back the rivers, a drought in dragon's form.

Indra fortifies himself by drinking three bowls of soma, then strikes. The hymn is full of strange, vivid images. Vṛtra, 'handless and footless', still fights. His mother Dānu lies over him like a cow over her calf, and Indra strikes her too. When the monster falls, the imprisoned waters flow over his body 'like lowing cows', streaming down to the sea.

The epithet Vṛtrahan, 'Vṛtra-slayer', becomes Indra's most characteristic title, and the fight is retold, expanded and moralised through the Brāhmaṇas and epics.

image.file: File:Indra kills Vrttirasura (story from Rik Veda, featured in Bhagavatha).jpg
image.caption: Indra slaying Vṛtra, book illustration published 1916

versions.title: Baal Defeats Sea
versions.teaser: Baal smashes Prince Sea and wins the right to a palace.
versions.text:
In the Baal Cycle from Ugarit, the god El favours Yam, 'Sea', also called Judge River, and Yam sends messengers to the divine assembly demanding that Baal be handed over as his slave. The gods cower, heads on their knees; Baal rebukes them and goes out to fight. He strikes Yam down and scatters him, and the cry goes up: 'Yam is dead! Baal shall be king!'

Other Ugaritic lines recall that Baal also crushed Litan, 'the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads'.

That description turns up almost word for word in the Hebrew Bible. Isaiah 27:1 promises that YHWH will punish 'Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent', and Psalm 74 praises the God who 'broke the heads of the dragons on the waters'. The old Canaanite combat survived by changing its hero.

versions.title: Set Spears Apep
versions.teaser: Every night the sun's boat is ambushed by a giant snake.
versions.text:
The Egyptian serpent fight never ends. Each night the sun god Ra sails his barque through the underworld, and each night the vast serpent Apep (Apophis), the embodiment of chaos, rises to swallow it, sometimes drinking up the river so that the boat runs aground.

Standing at the prow is Set, the god of storms and deserts, whose unruly violence is here put to good use. In texts and vignettes he drives a spear into the serpent's coils, and the sun sails on to rise at dawn. The cat of Ra, in the Book of the Dead, cuts off Apep's head with a knife under a sacred tree.

Priests helped. The Book of Overthrowing Apep in the Bremner-Rhind Papyrus prescribes making a wax snake, spitting on it, trampling it and burning it, day after day, to keep the cosmos going.
versions.caveat: Set is a storm god but his role against Apep is one of several; in later periods he was himself demonised and even identified with Apep.

image.file: File:Barque solaire contre Apopi.jpg
image.caption: Set spears Apep from the prow of Ra's solar boat; funerary papyrus of Herouben

versions.title: Zeus and Typhon
versions.teaser: A hundred snake heads against the thunderbolts of Zeus.
versions.text:
After the Titans were defeated, Gaia bore one last challenger, Typhon. Hesiod describes him with a hundred snake heads flickering dark tongues, eyes flashing fire, and voices that made every kind of sound: the speech of gods, the bellowing of a bull, the roar of a lion, the yelp of puppies, a hissing that echoed off the mountains.

Had Zeus not noticed in time, says Hesiod, Typhon would have become king of gods and men. Zeus thundered; the earth, sea and sky boiled; even Hades trembled. Then he leapt from Olympus, burned all the monstrous heads with his lightning, and flung the lamed creature into Tartarus.

From Typhon come the wild, useless winds that wreck ships and flatten crops. Later authors placed him under Mount Etna, still smouldering.

versions.title: Susanoo and the Eight-Headed Serpent
versions.teaser: The banished storm god gets eight heads drunk, then cuts them off.
versions.text:
Exiled from heaven for his outrages, the storm god Susanoo comes down in Izumo beside the river Hi. There he finds an old couple weeping over their daughter Kushinadahime. The serpent Yamata no Orochi, with eight heads and eight tails, eyes red as winter cherries, its body stretching over eight valleys and eight hills, has eaten seven of their eight daughters and is coming for the last.

Susanoo turns the girl into a comb and puts her in his hair. He has the parents brew strong sake eight times over and set it out in eight vats behind a fence with eight gates. The serpent comes, dips a head into each vat, drinks, and falls asleep. Susanoo hacks it to pieces until the river runs red.

In the middle tail his sword chips on something hard: the sword Kusanagi, which he presents to his sister Amaterasu.

image.file: File:Susanoo-no-Mikoto-slays-Yamata-no-Orochi-in-Izumo-By-Tsukioka-Yoshitoshi.png
image.caption: Susanoo slays Yamata no Orochi in Izumo, woodblock print by Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, 1887

versions.title: Thor and the World Serpent
versions.teaser: Thor hooks the Midgard Serpent once; at Ragnarök they finish it.
versions.text:
Jörmungandr, Loki's child, was flung by Odin into the ocean, where he grew until he encircled the whole world and bit his own tail. Thor meets him three times.

Once, in the hall of the giant Útgarða-Loki, he tries to lift a grey cat and manages only one paw; it turns out the cat was the Midgard Serpent in disguise. Then, fishing with the giant Hymir, Thor baits a hook with an ox head and hauls the serpent up to the gunwale. Their eyes meet, the serpent spitting poison, Thor raising his hammer, until the terrified Hymir cuts the line.

The third meeting is at Ragnarök. Thor kills the serpent at last, walks nine paces away from it, and falls dead from its venom. The world's defender and the world's encircler end together.

image.file: File:NKS 1867 4to, 93v, Thor and Jörmungandr.jpg
image.caption: Thor hooks the Midgard Serpent while Hymir watches; Icelandic manuscript NKS 1867 4to, c. 1760

versions.title: Perun Against Veles
versions.teaser: A modern reconstruction: thunder on the oak, serpent at its roots.
versions.text:
The Russian Primary Chronicle names Perun as the chief god of Kiev in 980, and the Rus' swore treaties by Perun and by Volos (Veles), 'god of cattle'. Beyond that the written record is thin.

In the 1970s the linguists Vyacheslav Ivanov and Vladimir Toporov proposed that a whole myth lay hidden in later Slavic folklore, place names and charms. In their reconstruction Perun, the thunderer, sits at the top of the world tree, while his serpentine enemy, Veles, lurks among its roots by the water. Veles steals Perun's cattle, or his wife, and hides behind trees, stones and animals. Perun hunts him, striking with thunderbolts until he flees back to the underworld, and the rain that follows is the reward.

It is elegant and much quoted. It is also a scholarly model rather than a story anyone wrote down.
sources: V. V. Ivanov and V. N. Toporov, Issledovaniya v oblasti slavyanskikh drevnostey (1974)
versions.caveat: The Perun–Veles combat is a modern reconstruction from fragments; no medieval source narrates it.

concepts.summary: The storm god rarely fights bare-handed. His weapon — hammer, club, axe, or bolt of fire — is often a named character in its own right, crafted by a divine smith, lost, stolen, or won back. Many peoples in Europe, Africa and Asia also believed that ancient stone axes turned up by the plough were thunderbolts that had fallen from the sky, and kept them as protection against lightning. The shared image probably reflects both inheritance within language families and the simple fact that lightning looks like something thrown.

versions.title: Baal's Two Clubs
versions.teaser: Two named clubs leap from Baal's hands 'like an eagle'.
versions.text:
When Baal hesitates before his fight with Sea, the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis encourages him and makes him two clubs, giving each a name that is also a spell. The first is Yagrush, 'Chaser': 'Chaser, drive Yam from his throne!' It swoops from Baal's hand like an eagle and strikes Yam on the shoulders, but Yam does not fall. The second is Ayamur, 'Expeller': 'Expeller, drive Yam from his throne!' It strikes Yam between the eyes, and Sea collapses to the ground.

The weapons are almost characters, addressed and dispatched like servants.

Baal's image in art makes the same point. The famous stele from Ugarit in the Louvre shows him striding, mace raised above his head, while in his other hand a spear sprouts into a plant, lightning and the rain it brings in a single gesture.

image.file: File:Baal thunderbolt Louvre AO15775.jpg
image.caption: Stele of Baal with thunderbolt, from Ugarit, c. 15th–13th century BCE, Louvre AO 15775

versions.title: The Cyclopes' Thunderbolt
versions.teaser: Zeus got his lightning as a thank-you gift from prisoners.
versions.text:
Hesiod explains where Zeus found his weapon. The three Cyclopes, Brontes, Steropes and Arges, 'Thunder', 'Lightning' and 'Bright', were sons of Earth and Sky, one-eyed smiths imprisoned underground by their father. When Zeus freed them, they remembered the kindness and gave him thunder, the blazing lightning bolt and the flash, which before then had lain hidden in the earth. 'Trusting in these,' says Hesiod, 'he rules mortals and immortals.'

In art the keraunos is a spindle of flame, pointed at both ends, often with little wings. Zeus rarely lends it. Where lightning struck the ground, Greeks built a small enclosure, since the spot now belonged to the god.

When Apollo's son Asclepius raised the dead and Zeus struck him down, Apollo took revenge not on Zeus but on the Cyclopes who had made the bolt.

versions.title: The Vajra from a Sage's Bones
versions.teaser: Indra's thunderbolt was made from a willing sage's spine.
versions.text:
The Rigveda says the craftsman god Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned Indra's vajra, the 'hard' or 'shattering' weapon, golden and many-edged, before his fight with Vṛtra.

Later tradition tells a more poignant story. When the demon Vṛtra could not be harmed by any existing weapon, the gods learned that only a weapon made from the bones of the ascetic Dadhīci would do. They went and asked him for his body. Dadhīci agreed, gave up his life through yoga, and the gods had the vajra shaped from his bones; with it Indra won. The story is told in the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

The vajra became one of Asia's great symbols. In Buddhism it stands for indestructible enlightenment, as in the name Vajrayāna, and the Tibetan dorje, held in a monk's hand during ritual, is the thunderbolt tamed into a teaching.

image.caption: Vajra (Tibetan dorje), gilt copper alloy, eastern Tibet or China, 18th–19th century, LACMA

versions.title: The Thunder God's Drums
versions.teaser: Han painters showed thunder as a strongman beating a ring of drums.
versions.text:
In early China thunder was not a thrown weapon but a sound made on purpose. The Han-dynasty philosopher Wang Chong, a rationalist who enjoyed debunking popular beliefs, describes how painters of his day depicted it: a row of drums linked together, and a strong man, the Thunder Lord, pulling them with his left hand and striking with a hammer in his right. The rumbling was the drumming; lightning was the fire of the blows.

Wang Chong thought this absurd; thunder, he argued, was a kind of fire, born of the clash of yin and yang. But the image lasted. Later Leigong, the Duke of Thunder, is shown with a bird's beak and wings, a hammer and chisel in his hands and drums on his back, and he punishes secret crimes. Being struck by lightning was widely taken as a sign of hidden guilt.
sources: Wang Chong, Lunheng, chapter 'Lei xu' (1st century CE)

versions.title: Thor's Hammer Stolen
versions.teaser: To recover Mjölnir, Thor must go to a giant's wedding as the bride.
versions.text:
Thor wakes one morning to find Mjölnir gone. Loki borrows Freyja's feather cloak and flies to the giant Þrymr, who admits he has buried the hammer eight leagues deep and will return it only if Freyja is given to him as his wife. Freyja's refusal is so furious that her necklace bursts.

Heimdall proposes a solution Thor hates: dress him as the bride. Veiled and wearing the necklace, with Loki as his maid, Thor goes to Jötunheim, where at the wedding feast he eats a whole ox, eight salmon and all the dainties meant for the women, and drinks three casks of mead. Loki explains that Freyja has been too eager to eat for eight nights.

Then, by custom, the hammer is laid in the bride's lap to hallow the marriage. Thor's heart laughs within him, and the wedding party ends badly for the giants.

versions.title: Ṣàngó's Double Axe
versions.teaser: Thunderstones in the fields are the axes Ṣàngó has hurled down.
versions.text:
Ṣàngó, the Yoruba god of thunder, was in tradition an early king of Oyo, fiery and magnificent, who could breathe flame and command lightning. His emblem is the double-headed axe, carved on the dance staffs, called oṣé Ṣàngó, carried by his devotees. On them a kneeling woman often balances the axe on her head, so that the thunder rests on the head of the worshipper.

When lightning strikes, Yoruba say Ṣàngó has thrown his thunderstones, edùn àrá, down to earth. The smooth prehistoric stone celts that farmers dig up are these very stones, and they are kept in wooden bowls in his shrines. After a strike, his priests came to search for the stone in the damaged house.

Through the Atlantic slave trade Ṣàngó travelled to Cuba and Brazil as Changó and Xangô, double axe and all.
sources: Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (1921)

image.file: File:Brooklyn Museum 79.27 Dance Wand Oshe Shango.jpg
image.caption: Oṣé Ṣàngó dance wand with double-axe motif, Yoruba, late 19th or early 20th century, Brooklyn Museum

concepts.summary: Twins are uncanny: two lives from one birth, alike yet different. Myth uses them for the paired forces of the world — morning and evening, life and death, good and evil — and often for rescuers who arrive on horseback or by sea. Indo-European traditions share a set of divine twin horsemen, the Vedic Aśvins and Greek Dioskouroi being the clearest cognates. Elsewhere twin myths arose independently and take very different forms: rival brothers who make the world between them, or sacred twins honoured by an entire people.

versions.title: Shu and Tefnut
versions.teaser: The first twins came from the creator's sneeze.
versions.text:
In the creation account of Heliopolis, the self-created god Atum, alone in the primeval waters, produced the first pair of gods from his own body. The Pyramid Texts say he sneezed out Shu and spat out Tefnut; the names themselves echo the sounds, for ishesh is 'sneeze' and tef 'spit'. Another utterance gives a cruder version involving his hand.

Shu is dry air and light, Tefnut moisture, and together they are the first male and female, the start of every other pairing in Egyptian cosmology. They in turn produce Geb and Nut, earth and sky.

A later text tells that the twins once became lost in the dark waters. Atum sent his Eye to find them, and when they were brought back, he wept with joy, and his tears became the first human beings.

versions.title: The Aśvins, Horsemen of Dawn
versions.teaser: Twin horsemen who rescue shipwrecks and fit iron legs.
versions.text:
The Aśvins, 'the horsemen', also called the Nāsatyas, are twin gods who race across the sky ahead of Dawn in a three-wheeled golden chariot. Their hymns in the Rigveda are catalogues of rescues. They save Bhujyu, abandoned in the ocean, carrying him home in winged ships over three days and nights. They restore the old sage Cyavana to youth. When the warrior woman Viśpalā loses a leg in battle, they give her an iron one, so that she can run again.

They are healers and wonder-workers, and in the Brāhmaṇas they have to fight for their share of the soma sacrifice, since the other gods think physicians too low for it.

They are also among the oldest attested Indo-Iranian gods: a Mitanni treaty with the Hittites around 1350 BCE invokes the Nāsatya gods as witnesses.
sources: Treaty of Šuppiluliuma I and Šattiwaza

image.file: File:Birth of the Celestial Twins, Folio from a Harivamsha (Lineage of Vishnu) LACMA M.83.1.7 (1 of 2).jpg
image.caption: Birth of the Celestial Twins, folio from a Mughal Harivaṃśa, Lahore, c. 1585–90, LACMA

versions.title: Castor and Polydeuces
versions.teaser: One twin was mortal, so they share immortality day by day.
versions.text:
The Dioskouroi, 'youths of Zeus', are Castor the horse-tamer and Polydeuces the boxer, brothers of Helen. In the usual story their mother Leda bore them in the same birth, but Polydeuces was son of Zeus and immortal, Castor son of the mortal Tyndareus.

When Castor was killed in a feud with their cousins, Polydeuces begged Zeus not to let him outlive his brother. Zeus gave him a choice: live forever on Olympus alone, or share his immortality. He chose to share, and so the twins spend alternate days among the gods and beneath the earth. Pindar tells it in his tenth Nemean ode; the Odyssey already knows that they 'live on alternate days'.

Sailors in a storm prayed to them, and the twin flames of St Elmo's fire on a mast meant the Dioskouroi had come aboard.

image.file: File:Castor and Pollux, archaic relief, AM of Delphi, 201363.jpg
image.caption: The Dioskouroi on a cattle raid, metope of the Sicyonian Treasury at Delphi, c. 560 BCE

versions.title: Twin Sons of Time
versions.teaser: Good and evil as twins: the firstborn would be king.
versions.text:
Zarathustra's own hymns, the Gāthās, speak of 'the two spirits, who at the beginning were known as twins', one choosing the good, the other the evil. The line inspired a remarkable myth.

According to Zurvanism, a strand of Sasanian Zoroastrianism described by Armenian and Syriac Christian writers, the primordial god Zurvan, 'Time', sacrificed for a thousand years to have a son. At last he doubted, and from that doubt he conceived twins: Ohrmazd from his offering, Ahriman from his doubt. Zurvan vowed to make the firstborn king. Ohrmazd understood this and told his brother, so Ahriman tore open the womb and came out first. 'My son is fragrant and bright,' said Zurvan, 'and you are dark and stinking.' Bound by his oath, he gave Ahriman nine thousand years of rule, after which Ohrmazd would reign.

Orthodox Zoroastrians rejected the whole idea.
sources: Eznik of Kołb, Against the Sects (5th century)
versions.caveat: The Zurvan myth is known mainly from hostile Christian writers and was a heterodox strand, not mainstream Zoroastrian doctrine.

versions.title: The Hero Twins of Xibalba
versions.teaser: Two ballplayers outwit the Lords of Death in their own house.
versions.text:
In the Popol Vuh, the brothers Hunahpu and Xbalanque are conceived when the skull of their father, hanging in a calabash tree in Xibalba, the underworld, spits into the hand of the maiden Xquic. Tormented by their jealous half-brothers, they turn them into monkeys.

Summoned to play ball against the Lords of Death, as their father had been before them, the twins pass every trial: the House of Knives, the House of Cold, the House of Jaguars, the House of Bats, where Hunahpu loses his head and the game continues with a squash in its place. Knowing they will be burned, they let it happen, return as wandering performers, and dazzle the lords by sacrificing and reviving each other. The lords beg to be sacrificed too. The twins kill them and do not bring them back.

Then they rise into the sky as the sun and the moon.
versions.caveat: The Popol Vuh was written down in the 16th century, though Classic Maya vases show the twins centuries earlier.

versions.title: Sapling and Flint
versions.teaser: One twin made rivers flow both ways; his brother spoiled them.
versions.text:
After Sky Woman fell from the upper world and landed on the Great Turtle's back, her daughter bore twins. The good-minded Sapling (in Mohawk, Teharonhiawako, among other names) was born the normal way. His brother Flint (Tawiskaron) burst out through her side, killing her.

The twins then shaped the world between them. Sapling made gentle landscapes, rivers with two currents so that canoes could travel either way without paddling, and useful plants and animals. Flint made rapids and cliffs, thorns on the bushes, and made the rivers flow one way only. In some tellings he shut the animals up in a cave, and Sapling let them out.

Finally the brothers fought, and Sapling won, sending Flint into the earth or the west. Versions differ from nation to nation, but the balance of the two minds runs through them all.
sources: David Cusick, Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations (1827)
J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology (1903, 1928)
versions.caveat: Tellings vary among the Mohawk, Onondaga, Seneca and other nations; names and details are not uniform.

versions.title: Ìbejì, the Sacred Twins
versions.teaser: When a twin dies, a small carved figure is fed and dressed.
versions.text:
The Yoruba have one of the highest natural twinning rates in the world, and twins, ìbejì, are regarded as sacred and bring good fortune to their families. The firstborn is named Táíwò, 'the one who tastes the world', sent ahead by the younger, Kẹ́hìndé, 'the one who comes after', who is considered the elder because he sends his sibling out first to see if the world is good.

If a twin dies, the family commissions a carver to make an ère ìbejì, a small wooden figure that stands for the lost child. The mother washes it, feeds it, dresses it, rubs it with camwood and carries it with the surviving twin, so the pair stays whole. Old figures often have their faces worn smooth by generations of loving handling.

There are thousands in museums; each one was a child.

image.file: File:Ere Ibeji, Nigeria, Benin, Brücke Museum Berlin, 64963, view a.jpg
image.caption: Ère ìbejì memorial figure for a deceased twin, Yoruba, 19th–20th century

concepts.summary: The trickster is a clever, greedy, shape-shifting boundary-crosser who breaks rules, steals, lies, and often gives humanity something precious by accident or theft. He may be a god, an animal or a culture hero, and he frequently gets caught by his own tricks. Tricksters appear on every inhabited continent, and their similarities are best explained by shared human delight in the underdog who outwits power, not by common descent. Paul Radin and Carl Jung made the figure famous as a universal type; more recent scholars warn against flattening very different traditions into one archetype.

versions.title: Hermes Steals the Cattle
versions.teaser: Born at dawn, a thief by evening, and lying to Zeus by morning.
versions.text:
The Homeric Hymn to Hermes tells the god's first day. Born at dawn in a cave on Mount Kyllene, by noon Hermes has climbed out of his cradle, found a tortoise, scooped it out and strung it with gut to invent the lyre. By evening he is hungry for meat.

He goes to Pieria and steals fifty of Apollo's cattle, driving them backwards so their tracks point the wrong way, and wearing sandals of twigs to disguise his own feet. He slaughters two, invents the method of making fire, and is back in his cradle, 'like a newborn baby', before sunrise.

Apollo drags him before Zeus, and the baby swears he doesn't even know what a cow is. Zeus laughs out loud. The quarrel ends when Hermes plays the lyre and Apollo, entranced, trades the cattle for it. Theft, music and commerce are born together.

image.file: File:De jonge Mercurius steelt runderen van Apollo's kudde, SK-A-3966.jpg
image.caption: The young Mercury steals cattle from Apollo's herd, painting by Girolamo da Santacroce, c. 1530–50, Rijksmuseum

versions.title: Loki and the Giant Builder
versions.teaser: Loki saves the gods' bargain by becoming a mare.
versions.text:
A mason offers to build the gods a wall around Asgard in a single winter. His price: Freyja, the sun and the moon. On Loki's advice the gods agree, confident he will fail, and allow him the help of his stallion Svaðilfari. But the horse hauls stones at an astonishing rate, and three days before summer the wall is nearly finished.

The gods, furious, threaten Loki with a terrible death unless he fixes it. That night a mare comes out of the woods and whinnies at the stallion, who breaks his harness and chases her into the forest all night. The work is not finished, the builder shows himself as a giant in rage, and Thor kills him.

Some time later Loki gives birth to a grey foal with eight legs: Sleipnir, the finest of horses, which becomes Odin's mount.

versions.title: The Monkey King in Heaven
versions.teaser: A stone monkey eats the peaches of immortality and wrecks heaven.
versions.text:
Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, is born from a stone egg on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. He learns magic from a Daoist master: seventy-two transformations and a cloud-somersault that carries him thousands of miles in one leap. From the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea he takes the iron staff that shrinks to the size of a needle.

The Jade Emperor tries to keep him quiet with a grand title, then with a job minding the heavenly horses, then guarding the orchard of immortal peaches, which he eats. He also swallows Laozi's elixir pills and gatecrashes a banquet. All heaven's armies cannot subdue him.

Finally the Buddha makes a bet: jump out of my palm. Wukong leaps to five great pillars at the end of the world and marks one. They are the Buddha's fingers. He is pinned under a mountain for five hundred years.
sources: Wu Cheng'en (attributed), Journey to the West (Xiyouji), chapters 1–7
versions.caveat: Journey to the West is a 16th-century literary novel drawing on earlier folk and religious tradition, not a scripture.

image.file: File:孫悟空 Sun Wukong or Monkey King and Shakyamuni Buddha 01.jpg
image.caption: Sun Wukong, illustration by Matsukawa Hanzan in a book published in Osaka, 1864

versions.title: Māui Snares the Sun
versions.teaser: The youngest son slows the sun and fishes up an island.
versions.text:
Māui-tikitiki-a-Taranga was born prematurely and thrown into the sea wrapped in his mother's topknot, but survived to become the cleverest and most troublesome of heroes.

The days were too short to finish any work, so Māui and his brothers plaited ropes, travelled to the pit where the sun rises, and snared it as it climbed out. Māui beat it with the jawbone of his ancestress Murirangawhenua until it was lamed and had to crawl across the sky, as it does now. With the same jawbone as a fishhook, baited with his own blood, he hauled up the North Island, Te Ika-a-Māui, 'Māui's Fish'. He tricked the fire goddess Mahuika out of her fingernails of flame.

Finally he tried to win immortality by crawling through the body of the death goddess Hine-nui-te-pō as she slept. A fantail laughed, she woke, and Māui died.
versions.caveat: Māui stories are told across Polynesia (Hawaiian, Tongan, Samoan and others) with many regional differences; this is the Māori form.

image.file: File:Maui Snaring the Sun by Arman Tateos Manookian, c. 1927, drawing, Honolulu Museum of Art.jpg
image.caption: Maui Snaring the Sun, drawing by Arman Tateos Manookian, c. 1927 (a Hawaiian rendering of the story), Honolulu Museum of Art

versions.title: Anansi Buys the Stories
versions.teaser: The spider pays the sky god's price and wins every story.
versions.text:
Once all stories belonged to Nyame, the sky god. Kwaku Ananse, the spider, asked to buy them. Nyame laughed: great towns had tried and failed. The price was Onini the python, Osebo the leopard, Mmoboro the hornets and Mmoatia the fairy.

Ananse caught each by a trick. He argued aloud with himself about whether the python was longer than a palm branch, until Onini lay down beside it to prove it, and was tied fast. He dug a pit on the leopard's path. He poured water over the hornets' nest and invited them to shelter from the 'rain' in his gourd. He made a sticky doll holding a bowl of yams, and the fairy, offended that it would not answer her, slapped it and stuck.

Nyame, impressed, announced before his court: 'From today these are Ananse's stories.' And so they are called, anansesɛm.

versions.title: Èṣù's Two-Coloured Cap
versions.teaser: A cap red on one side and black on the other ends a friendship.
versions.text:
Èṣù is the Yoruba messenger of the gods, the guardian of crossroads, and the one who carries sacrifices to heaven. He is not evil, whatever missionaries said, but he punishes those who neglect him, and he loves to test people.

In a widely told story two farmers are inseparable friends, their fields side by side, and forget to honour Èṣù. So he walks down the path between their fields wearing a cap painted one colour on one side and another colour on the other. When they discuss the stranger, one insists his cap was black, the other that it was red. Each calls the other a liar, the argument becomes a fight, and they are hauled before the king. Èṣù appears, shows them the cap, and laughs.

The lesson is not only about Èṣù. Every truth depends on where you stand.
versions.caveat: The cap's colours vary between tellings (often red and black, sometimes red and white or blue).

versions.title: Wakdjunkaga's Quarrelling Hands
versions.teaser: A trickster whose right arm and left arm fight over a buffalo.
versions.text:
The Ho-Chunk trickster cycle, dictated to the anthropologist Paul Radin by Sam Blowsnake, follows Wakdjunkaga, 'the Tricky One', through a string of misadventures that are funny, obscene and oddly profound.

At the start he is a chief who abandons his war party and wanders off alone. He kills a buffalo, and while he is butchering it, his left arm grabs at the meat. The right arm fights it off; the left arm fights back, until it is cut and bleeding and Wakdjunkaga cries, 'Why have I done this?' He does not yet know his own body. Later he tells his anus to guard roasting ducks, is robbed, and burns it in punishment, and then unknowingly eats his own flesh.

By the end of the cycle he has learned, piece by piece, what a body is and how the world works, and he removes obstacles from the Mississippi for the people who will come.
sources: Paul Radin, The Trickster: A Study in American Indian Mythology (1956)

concepts.summary: Many mythologies remember a great war among the gods themselves: older powers against younger, one divine family against another, order against disorder. The winners become the gods people actually worship; the losers are imprisoned below, demoted to demons, or absorbed by treaty. The Hurrian-Hittite, Babylonian and Greek succession myths are so alike that most scholars accept Near Eastern influence on Hesiod, while Indo-European comparativists see an inherited pattern in the Norse and Indian wars between divine clans. The motif also reflects real politics: conquests, alliances and the merging of cults.

versions.title: Kingship in Heaven
versions.teaser: Four generations of gods overthrow each other, one bite at a time.
versions.text:
The Hittite 'Song of Kumarbi', translated from a Hurrian original, tells of kings in heaven who each rule nine years. First Alalu is king, until his cupbearer Anu, the Sky, overthrows him and drives him down to the dark earth. Then Anu's cupbearer Kumarbi rebels. As Anu flees upward, Kumarbi catches him by the feet, drags him down and bites off his genitals.

Kumarbi rejoices, until Anu tells him the truth: he has swallowed the Sky's seed and is now pregnant with three terrible gods, chief among them the Storm God Teshub. Kumarbi spits some out, but Teshub is born anyway, and in the damaged later columns he apparently takes the throne.

Kumarbi never accepts defeat. In the sequel, the Song of Ullikummi, he fathers a stone giant to challenge the storm god. Greek readers will recognise the plot: sky, castration, swallowed children and a storm god who rises last.
versions.caveat: The tablets are badly broken at key points, so the details of Teshub's victory are reconstructed.

versions.title: Marduk Against Tiamat
versions.teaser: The young gods are too noisy, and their ancestors decide to kill them.
versions.text:
In Enūma Eliš the first powers are Apsu, the fresh water, and Tiamat, the sea. The younger gods they produce are so noisy that Apsu cannot sleep and resolves to destroy them. The clever Ea learns of the plan, casts a spell on Apsu and kills him.

Tiamat, at first patient, is stirred to revenge. She creates an army of monsters, serpents with venom for blood, and puts the god Kingu at its head, fastening the Tablet of Destinies on his chest. The gods are terrified; Anu and Ea both turn back.

Marduk, Ea's son, agrees to fight on one condition: that he be made king. Armed with bow, net and the four winds, he drives a wind into Tiamat's open mouth, shoots an arrow into her belly, and splits her body in two like a dried fish, making sky from one half and earth from the other. Humanity is made from Kingu's blood.

versions.title: Devas and Asuras
versions.teaser: Brothers, children of one father, fighting forever over the sacrifice.
versions.text:
The Brāhmaṇas, prose ritual manuals attached to the Vedas, return again and again to a formula: 'The devas and the asuras, both children of Prajāpati, contended.' The gods and their rivals are brothers, and they fight over the worlds, the sacrifice and speech itself.

The asuras are often stronger, more numerous, and at first winning. The gods win by knowledge: they discover the correct rite, the right metre, the secret of the offering, and the asuras, who perform the sacrifice wrongly or arrogantly, lose. In one story the asuras make their offerings into their own mouths, while the gods make them to each other, and so win.

The word asura itself is revealing. In the oldest Rigveda it is an honorific applied even to Varuṇa and Indra; later it means 'demon'. In Iran, the cognate ahura became the name of the supreme god, Ahura Mazdā.

versions.title: The Titanomachy
versions.teaser: Ten years of war, until the Hundred-Handers throw three hundred rocks.
versions.text:
Zeus and his siblings, rescued from their father Kronos's stomach, go to war against the Titans for rule of the world. For ten years they fight from Mount Olympus, the Titans from Mount Othrys, and neither side gives way.

On Gaia's advice, Zeus frees the Hundred-Handers, Kottos, Briareos and Gyges, whom Ouranos had imprisoned beneath the earth, and gives them nectar and ambrosia to revive their strength. Hesiod's battle is cosmic: the sea roars, the earth groans, Zeus hurls lightning until forests burn and the ocean boils. The Hundred-Handers throw three hundred rocks at once, burying the Titans in shadow, then chain them in Tartarus, as far below the earth as the earth is below heaven. A bronze anvil, Hesiod adds, would fall nine days and nights to get there.

The Hundred-Handers stay as their guards.

image.file: File:Joachim Wtewael - The Battle Between the Gods and the Titans - WGA25902.jpg
image.caption: The Battle Between the Gods and the Titans, painting by Joachim Wtewael, c. 1600

versions.title: The Yellow Emperor and Chiyou
versions.teaser: Chiyou summons wind and rain; the Yellow Emperor sends Drought.
versions.text:
The Shanhaijing, the Classic of Mountains and Seas, preserves a fragment of a divine war. Chiyou, a fearsome figure later remembered as the inventor of weapons, made war on the Yellow Emperor, Huangdi. Huangdi ordered the winged dragon Yinglong to attack him on the plain of Jizhou and to store up water. But Chiyou asked the Wind Lord and the Rain Master to unleash a great storm.

Huangdi then sent down a heavenly woman called Ba, the spirit of drought. The rain stopped, and Chiyou was killed. But Ba could not return to heaven, and wherever she lives, no rain falls. People drive her away by clearing the ditches and commanding, 'Goddess, go north!'

Later historians, beginning with Sima Qian, rewrote the war as history: a battle at Zhuolu between human rulers, from which Chinese civilisation traced its founding.

image.file: File:Chi You.gif
image.caption: Chiyou, rubbing of a Han-dynasty stone relief

versions.title: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired
versions.teaser: Lug's sling-stone drives Balor's deadly eye through the back of his head.
versions.text:
The Tuatha Dé Danann, the divine people of Ireland, suffer under the oppression of the Fomoire, whose king Bres, half-Fomorian, is so stingy that his guests leave his hall with ungreased knives and breath that smells of nothing.

The young god Lug arrives at Tara as master of every art and leads the rebellion. The Dé Danann craftsmen forge weapons, their physicians fill a healing well that restores the fallen, and the two peoples meet at Mag Tuired.

The Fomorian champion is Balor, whose eye is so poisonous that it takes four men to lift its lid with a polished handle, and any army it looks on is destroyed. When the lid is raised, Lug casts a sling-stone that drives the eye out through the back of his head, where it falls on his own troops.

The Morrígan ends the tale with a prophecy of the world's end.
sources: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired)
versions.caveat: The text was written by Christian monks, who framed the Tuatha Dé as ancient inhabitants of Ireland rather than gods.

versions.title: Ahriman's Assault
versions.teaser: The Evil Spirit bursts through the sky and poisons creation.
versions.text:
In the Zoroastrian cosmology of the Bundahišn, history is a war between Ohrmazd, the Wise Lord, and Ahriman, the Destructive Spirit. Ohrmazd first creates the world in a perfect, motionless spiritual form, and recites a sacred prayer that stuns Ahriman for three thousand years.

When Ahriman wakes, he attacks. He bursts through the sky like a snake, pierces the earth, fouls the waters with salt, withers the plants, and sends plague and death upon the first bull and the first man, Gayōmard. Each of Ohrmazd's heavenly powers, the Amahraspands, is now paired with a demon who opposes it, and every human being joins the war by choosing good thoughts, words and deeds.

The war has an end: after twelve thousand years, a saviour will raise the dead, molten metal will purify the world, and Ahriman will be destroyed.

versions.title: The Æsir–Vanir War
versions.teaser: The first war in the world ends in hostages and a truce.
versions.text:
Völuspá calls it 'the first war in the world'. It begins when the Æsir stab a mysterious woman, Gullveig, with spears and burn her three times in Odin's hall, and three times she is reborn. Odin then hurls his spear over the enemy host, and war breaks out with the Vanir, the gods of fertility. The Vanir break down the walls of Asgard.

Neither side can win, so they make peace and exchange hostages. The Vanir send Njörðr and his son Freyr, and Freyja comes too; the Æsir send Hœnir and wise Mímir. When the Vanir feel cheated by Hœnir's indecision, they behead Mímir and send the head back to Odin, who preserves it with herbs and consults it ever after.

In Snorri's telling, the gods seal the truce by spitting into a vat; from that spittle they make Kvasir, the wisest of beings.

image.file: File:Æsir-Vanir war by Frølich.jpg
image.caption: Odin hurls his spear over the Vanir host, illustration by Lorenz Frølich, published 1895

versions.title: Huitzilopochtli at Snake Mountain
versions.teaser: The war god is born fully armed to defend his mother.
versions.text:
At Coatepec, Snake Mountain, the goddess Coatlicue was sweeping when a ball of feathers fell from the sky. She tucked it into her waistband and found herself pregnant. Her daughter Coyolxauhqui and her four hundred sons, the Centzon Huitznahua, were outraged at the disgrace and resolved to kill her.

As they marched up the mountain, the child in her womb spoke to comfort her. At the moment they arrived, Huitzilopochtli was born, fully armed, his face painted, bearing the fire serpent Xiuhcoatl. He struck off Coyolxauhqui's head, and her body tumbled down the mountain and broke apart. Then he chased the four hundred around the mountain and slew most of them.

The Mexica built their Templo Mayor as Snake Mountain. In 1978 workers found at its foot a huge carved stone of Coyolxauhqui, dismembered, just as the story says.
sources: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 3

image.caption: Colour reconstruction of the dismembered Coyolxauhqui stone, Museo del Templo Mayor, Mexico City

concepts.summary: Gods are often immortal not by nature but by diet: they drink or eat something that mortals lack. Soma and haoma, ambrosia and nectar, the elixir of the Chinese immortals and the 'water of life' offered to Adapa all express the idea that eternal life is a substance that can be guarded, stolen or refused. The Indo-Iranian soma/haoma is a genuine shared inheritance, a real ritual drink whose identity is still debated; the other parallels probably arise independently, from the human habit of imagining life as something taken in at the mouth.

versions.title: Adapa Refuses the Bread of Life
versions.teaser: Warned to refuse poison, Adapa turns down immortality instead.
versions.text:
Adapa, the wise priest of the god Ea at Eridu, is fishing when the South Wind capsizes his boat. In anger he curses it and breaks its wing, and for seven days no wind blows over the land. Anu summons him to heaven to explain.

Ea gives him careful advice. Wear mourning, flatter the gatekeepers Tammuz and Gizzida, and above all, when they offer you the bread of death and the water of death, do not eat or drink. Adapa obeys. But Anu, softened by the gatekeepers, offers instead the bread of life and the water of life. Adapa refuses them.

Anu laughs: 'Why did you not eat or drink? Now you shall not live.' Whether Ea was mistaken or meant it all along is the puzzle of the story. Either way, humanity's chance at eternal life was turned down politely at the door.
sources: Adapa myth (Amarna tablet and Assyrian fragments)

image.file: File:Fragment of the Epic of Adapa, Akkadian, Mesopotamia, Neo-Assyrian period, c. 7th century BC, clay - Morgan Library & Museum - New York City - DSC06601.jpg
image.caption: Fragment of the Adapa myth from the library of Assurbanipal, 7th century BCE, Morgan Library & Museum

versions.title: We Have Drunk the Soma
versions.teaser: A pressed plant juice that made its drinkers feel like gods.
versions.text:
Soma was both a god and a drink: the juice of a mountain plant, pressed between stones, filtered through wool and mixed with milk, offered to the gods and drunk by the priests. The whole ninth book of the Rigveda is devoted to Soma Pavamāna, 'self-purifying', flowing through the sieve.

Its effects were extraordinary. In Rigveda 8.48 the singers exult: 'We have drunk the soma, we have become immortal, we have gone to the light, we have found the gods.' Indra drinks lakes of it before battle. In another hymn a drinker feels himself swelling larger than heaven and earth.

The myth says an eagle stole soma from heaven and brought it to Indra. Its botanical identity was lost long ago; ephedra, fly agaric and other candidates have been argued for decades, and no answer is agreed.
versions.caveat: The plant's identity is unknown and every proposed identification remains contested.

versions.title: Haoma, the Death-Averting
versions.teaser: Zarathustra meets a radiant being, the ritual drink in person.
versions.text:
In Iran the same drink, haoma, cognate with soma, is still prepared in Zoroastrian ritual. Its hymn in the Avesta, the Hōm Yašt, opens with Zarathustra tending the fire at dawn when a beautiful figure approaches: it is Haoma himself, who tells the prophet to press him and praise him. Haoma is called dūraoša, 'death-averting', and grants health, strong sons and victory.

Later Pahlavi texts add a cosmic dimension. In the sea Vourukasha grows the White Haoma, or Gōkarn, a tree whose juice will make the resurrected immortal at the end of time. Ahriman sends a lizard to gnaw at its roots, and ten fish circle it forever on guard.

In modern Parsi ritual the priests pound twigs of a plant, usually ephedra, with pomegranate and water, preserving a practice older than Zarathustra.

versions.title: Nectar, Ambrosia and Tantalus
versions.teaser: Gods bleed ichor because they never touch bread or wine.
versions.text:
The Olympians eat ambrosia and drink nectar, the only food of immortals. When Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in the Iliad, what flows is ichor, 'for they eat no bread, nor drink gleaming wine, and so they are bloodless and are called immortal'. Ambrosia can also be rubbed on the skin, used to preserve a corpse, or fed to divine horses.

The food is guarded jealously. Pindar tells that Tantalus, a mortal honoured at the gods' table, stole nectar and ambrosia to share with his drinking companions, and so was punished forever. Demeter, disguised as a nursemaid, anoints the baby Demophon with ambrosia and places him in the fire each night to burn away his mortality, until his horrified mother interrupts her.

Even the word ambrosia means simply 'not-mortal-ness', a name that makes the claim.

versions.title: Chang'e Steals the Elixir
versions.teaser: The archer's wife swallows his elixir and floats to the moon.
versions.text:
The great archer Yi, who shot down nine of the ten suns scorching the earth, obtained an elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, Xiwangmu, in her palace on Mount Kunlun. Before he could use it, his wife Heng'e, later called Chang'e, stole it, swallowed it and fled to the moon.

The Huainanzi, a Han compendium of the second century BCE, gives the story in a single wistful sentence: Yi was left grieving, with nothing he could do, 'for he did not know where the elixir came from'.

Later versions soften Chang'e, making her swallow it to keep it from a thief, and give her company in the Moon Palace: a jade hare pounding the elixir in a mortar, and a woodcutter endlessly chopping a cassia tree. At the Mid-Autumn Festival families still look for them in the full moon.
