image.caption: Chang'e flees to the moon, woodblock print by Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, before 1892

versions.title: Churning the Ocean of Milk
versions.teaser: Gods and demons churn the ocean together, then fight over the result.
versions.text:
Weakened, the gods need amṛta, the nectar of immortality, and the only way to get it is to churn the Ocean of Milk. They cannot do it alone, so they make a truce with the asuras. Mount Mandara serves as the churning rod, the serpent king Vāsuki as the rope, and Viṣṇu, as a giant tortoise, supports the mountain on his back.

From the ocean emerge wonders: the moon, the goddess Lakṣmī, a wish-granting cow, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, and also a deadly poison that Śiva drinks to save the world, which stains his throat blue. At last the physician Dhanvantari rises holding the pot of amṛta.

The asuras seize it. Viṣṇu appears as the enchantress Mohinī and serves it only to the gods. The demon Rāhu slips into line and drinks, but the Sun and Moon expose him; his head, now immortal, still swallows them in eclipses.

image.file: File:Churning of the ocean - Manthan.jpg
image.caption: The churning of the ocean, from the Razmnāma (Persian Mahābhārata), attributed to Fattu, c. 1598

versions.title: Iðunn's Apples
versions.teaser: Without their daily apples, the gods grow grey and wrinkled.
versions.text:
The Norse gods keep their youth by eating apples kept by the goddess Iðunn. Snorri tells how Loki, captured by the giant Þjazi in eagle form, is forced to promise to bring Iðunn out of Asgard. He lures her into a wood, saying he has found apples even better than hers; Þjazi swoops down and carries her off.

Without her, the gods quickly become grey and old. They trace the disappearance to Loki and threaten him with death. He borrows Freyja's falcon cloak, flies to Þjazi's hall, turns Iðunn into a nut, and flies home with her in his claws. Þjazi pursues as an eagle, but the gods light a fire of wood shavings under Asgard's walls and his feathers catch fire; the gods kill him.

Immortality here is not a nature but a supply chain, and it can be stolen.
versions.caveat: Iðunn's gift is food, not drink, and the apples themselves may be a later or learned detail.

image.file: File:Idun and the Apples by James Doyle Penrose, 1890.jpg
image.caption: Idun and the Apples, painting by James Doyle Penrose, 1890

concepts.summary: Where there is metalwork there is usually a god of the forge: a maker of weapons, jewels and palaces for other gods, often lame, ugly, marginal, or otherwise set apart from the beautiful immortals he equips. The smith god embodies a real social fact: smiths in many societies were respected, feared and slightly outside ordinary life, keepers of a craft close to magic. Some names are related, but most smith gods are independent creations, shaped by the same experience of fire turning rock into tools.

versions.title: Ptah Creates by Speech
versions.teaser: The god of craftsmen made the world by thinking and speaking.
versions.text:
Ptah of Memphis was the patron of sculptors, metalworkers and builders, shown as a mummiform man in a close-fitting cap, holding a sceptre. His high priest bore the title 'Greatest of the Directors of Craftsmanship'.

But the Memphite priests made Ptah far more than a craftsman. The text known as the Memphite Theology, carved on the Shabaka Stone around 700 BCE, claims that Ptah created the gods and the whole world through his heart and his tongue: he conceived things in thought and brought them into being by naming them. Even the creator Atum and his Ennead came into existence this way.

The Greeks later identified Ptah with Hephaestus. The difference is telling: the Greek smith labours sweating at an anvil, while Ptah's greatest work was done by a word.
sources: Memphite Theology (Shabaka Stone, British Museum EA 498)
versions.caveat: The text claims to copy an ancient worm-eaten original, but many scholars now date its composition to the late New Kingdom or to Shabaka's own reign.

image.file: File:The Shabaka Stone.JPG
image.caption: The Shabaka Stone, bearing the Memphite Theology, c. 700 BCE, British Museum

versions.title: Kothar and the Window
versions.teaser: The craftsman god argues with Baal about a window, and wins.
versions.text:
Kothar-wa-Khasis, 'Skilful-and-Wise', is the craftsman of the Ugaritic gods, whose workshops lie far away in Kaphtor, probably Crete, and Memphis. He makes Baal's weapons, a throne and couch and gifts of gold for the goddess Athirat, and eventually Baal's palace of silver, gold and lapis lazuli on Mount Saphon.

The building scene contains a charming quarrel. Kothar says the house needs a window. Baal refuses: his enemy Yam must not get in, and he fears for his daughters. Kothar replies calmly, 'You will come back to my word, Baal.' Baal refuses twice more, the palace is completed with a six-day fire that melts the precious metal into bricks, and then, having defeated his enemies, Baal changes his mind. The window is opened, and through it Baal gives his holy voice: thunder, and the rain.

The smith, of course, was right.

versions.title: Tvaṣṭṛ and the Ṛbhus
versions.teaser: Three craftsman brothers improve on the gods' master smith.
versions.text:
Tvaṣṭṛ, 'the Fashioner', is the Vedic artisan god. He forged Indra's vajra, shapes the embryo in the womb, and owns a marvellous cup from which the gods drink soma.

But the Rigveda also praises three rival craftsmen, the Ṛbhus, sons of Sudhanvan. They renewed their aged parents' youth, made a chariot that ran by itself for the Aśvins, and fashioned a cow from a hide. Their greatest feat was a challenge: they took Tvaṣṭṛ's single cup and made four from it. The gods were so impressed that the Ṛbhus, though born mortal, were given immortality and a share of the soma. Tvaṣṭṛ, according to one hymn, hid among the goddesses in embarrassment.

The story is an early piece of craft pride: skill good enough can raise a worker to heaven.

versions.title: Hephaestus Thrown from Heaven
versions.teaser: The lame smith god builds golden robots and a shield for Achilles.
versions.text:
Hephaestus is the one Olympian who works. He was thrown out of heaven twice, the Iliad says: once by Hera, ashamed that her son was born lame, when he fell into the sea and was sheltered by Thetis; once by Zeus, for taking his mother's side, when he fell all day and landed on Lemnos at sunset, barely alive.

His forge on Olympus is a wonder. He has twenty tripods that roll by themselves to the gods' assemblies, and golden maidservants 'like living girls', with minds and voices, who help him walk. When Thetis asks for armour for Achilles, he makes a shield showing the whole world: earth, sea and sky, a city at peace and a city at war, a wedding, a lawsuit, a harvest and a dance.

The gods still laugh at him limping round with the wine. He outlasts their laughter by making everything they use.

image.file: File:Edward Smith - Thetis Entreats Hephaestus, who is Supported on Two Artificial Golden Handmaids, to Provide Achilles with Armour, 1805.jpg
image.caption: Thetis entreats Hephaestus, supported by his golden handmaids, engraving by Edward Smith after Henry Fuseli, 1805

versions.title: Goibniu's Three Blows
versions.teaser: The Irish smith makes a spearhead with three strokes of the hammer.
versions.text:
In the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, the smith Goibniu promises that however long the war lasts, he will replace every broken spear and sword. He works with two companions: Luchta the wright, who makes shafts, and Credne the brazier, who makes rivets. Goibniu forges each spearhead with three blows. Luchta hurls the shaft into the socket, and Credne flings the rivets so they fly straight into their holes.

The Fomoire send a spy, Ruadán, son of Bres and Brigit. He takes a spear from the forge and wounds Goibniu with it, but the smith pulls it out and kills him, and Brigit's keening over her son is said to be the first keening heard in Ireland.

Later Irish tales give him a feast, the Fled Goibnenn, whose ale kept those who drank it from age and death.
sources: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired)
versions.caveat: Like the rest of the Irish mythological cycle, this was written down by Christian monks, centuries after the gods ceased to be worshipped.

versions.title: Svarog and the Fallen Tongs
versions.teaser: A chronicler's gloss makes a Slavic god the equal of Hephaestus.
versions.text:
Nearly everything known of Svarog comes from one passage. The Hypatian Codex of the Rus' chronicles includes a translation of the Byzantine historian John Malalas, and under the year 1114 it renders his account of early Egyptian kings with a native gloss: in the reign of Feost, whom the Egyptians called Svarog, tongs fell from the sky and men began to forge weapons, since before that they had fought with clubs and stones. Feost is Malalas's Hephaestus. The gloss then names his son as the Sun, Dazhbog.

That single equation, Svarog equals Hephaestus, has launched a great deal of speculation about a Slavic smith and sky god. Svarozhich, 'son of Svarog', appears separately in Western Slavic sources as a god worshipped at Rethra.

It is a reminder how thin the thread of pagan Slavic religion can be: sometimes one borrowed sentence.
sources: Hypatian Codex, entry for 1114 (translating John Malalas)
versions.caveat: Svarog's smithing role rests entirely on a chronicler's gloss equating him with Hephaestus; its reliability is debated.

versions.title: The Dwarves' Wager
versions.teaser: Two dwarf smiths forge the gods' treasures to win Loki's head.
versions.text:
Loki, as a prank, cuts off all of Sif's golden hair. Threatened by Thor, he goes to the dwarves, the Sons of Ivaldi, who forge new hair of real gold that will grow like her own, and also the folding ship Skíðblaðnir and Odin's spear Gungnir.

Then Loki bets his head that the dwarf Brokkr's brother Eitri cannot make three treasures as good. Eitri sets pigskin in the forge and tells Brokkr to pump the bellows without stopping. A fly bites Brokkr's hand, but out comes the golden boar Gullinbursti. Then gold; the fly bites his neck, and out comes the ring Draupnir, which drips eight rings like itself every ninth night. Then iron; the fly, Loki in disguise, bites his eyelid, Brokkr stops a moment to brush it away, and the hammer Mjölnir emerges with its handle a little short.

The gods judge the hammer best. Loki, losing, saves his head by arguing that Brokkr has no claim on his neck. Brokkr sews his lips shut instead.

versions.title: Ilmarinen Forges the Sampo
versions.teaser: The smith who hammered out the sky makes a magic mill.
versions.text:
Ilmarinen is the eternal smith of Finnish and Karelian song, who once forged the lid of the sky itself, 'with no trace of the hammer, no mark of the tongs'. When the North's formidable mistress Louhi promises him her daughter if he can make the Sampo, a mysterious object that grinds out grain, salt and money, he builds a forge in the land of Pohjola.

For days he works the bellows and fire, and from the flames come a crossbow that demands a head each day, a boat that seeks out war, a cow that spills its milk, a plough that tramples neighbours' fields. He breaks each one back into the fire. At last the Sampo rises, with its lid of many colours, and begins to grind.

Louhi locks it in a hill of copper behind nine locks, and the heroes' later attempt to steal it back shatters it at sea.
versions.caveat: The Kalevala sequence is Lönnrot's arrangement; in the folk songs the Sampo's forging and nature vary widely.

image.file: File:Joseph Alanen - The Forging of the Sampo.jpg
image.caption: The Forging of the Sampo, painting by Joseph Alanen, 1910–11

versions.title: Ògún Clears the Road
versions.teaser: When the gods came to earth, only iron could cut the way.
versions.text:
Ògún is the Yoruba god of iron, and so of hunters, warriors, blacksmiths and, today, drivers, mechanics and anyone whose livelihood depends on metal. In a well-known tradition, when the òrìṣà descended from heaven to the earth, they found the way blocked by impenetrable forest. The other gods failed to clear it. Ògún alone had an iron cutlass, and he hacked the path through. The grateful gods offered him kingship.

He later ruled the town of Ìrè but, in a terrible story, returned from war to find its people silent because of a ritual fast, took it as an insult and slaughtered them. In remorse he planted his sword in the ground and sank into the earth.

Oaths in Yoruba courts could be sworn on a piece of iron, in Ògún's name. The god of the road is also the god of the broken promise.
sources: Yoruba oral tradition and Ifá verses
Sandra T. Barnes (ed.), Africa's Ogun: Old World and New (1989)

concepts.summary: In the ancient Near East and beyond, the same goddess often rules both desire and battle: passion and fury, the two forces that most completely overwhelm human reason. Inanna/Ishtar is the great example, and her influence spread through Canaanite Anat and Astarte, and possibly to Greek Aphrodite, who kept faint martial traces. Elsewhere, as among the Irish and Norse, similar combinations probably arose independently from goddesses of sovereignty and death. Modern readers sometimes find the pairing paradoxical; ancient worshippers apparently found it obvious.

versions.title: Inanna, Lady of Battle
versions.teaser: Battle is her dance; love is her field; nobody refuses her.
versions.text:
Inanna, called Ishtar in Akkadian, is the goddess of sexual love and of war at once, and the morning and evening star. The hymns of Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon and priestess at Ur around 2300 BCE, praise her as a storm who 'rains fire', whose battle is 'the dance of Inanna'.

In Inanna and Ebih she destroys a mountain simply because it refused to bow to her. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet VI, she proposes marriage to Gilgamesh; he recites her list of discarded lovers, a shepherd turned into a wolf, a gardener turned into a frog or mole, and rejects her. In fury she demands that her father Anu send the Bull of Heaven against Uruk, threatening to break open the underworld and let the dead devour the living.

Kings claimed to be her lovers and her soldiers. The two roles were not in tension: both were about overwhelming power.

image.file: File:The Queen of the Night (The Burney Relief) - British Museum.jpg
image.caption: The 'Queen of the Night' (Burney Relief), Old Babylonian, c. 1800–1750 BCE, British Museum; often identified as Ishtar, though this is debated

versions.title: Hathor Becomes Sekhmet
versions.teaser: The goddess of love turns lion and must be tricked with red beer.
versions.text:
In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, found in the tombs of Tutankhamun and later kings, the aging sun god Ra learns that humanity is plotting against him. He sends his Eye, in the form of the goddess Hathor, to punish them. She becomes Sekhmet, the lioness, 'the Powerful One', and slaughters people in the desert, wading in their blood.

Ra relents, but she cannot be stopped. So he orders seven thousand jars of beer brewed and dyed red with ochre, and has them poured over the fields at night. At dawn the goddess sees what looks like a lake of blood, drinks it all, and returns drunk and peaceful, not recognising mankind.

Hathor was the golden goddess of love, music and drunkenness, Sekhmet the plague-bringer; they were two faces of one dangerous Eye. Her festivals of drunkenness remembered the night the world was saved by beer.

image.file: File:Statue of the goddess Sekhmet, granodiorite - Museo Egizio Turin C 250 p02.jpg
image.caption: Granodiorite statue of Sekhmet, reign of Amenhotep III, c. 1390–1353 BCE, Museo Egizio, Turin

versions.title: Anat's Slaughter
versions.teaser: Heads bounce like balls around the young goddess as she fights.
versions.text:
Anat, 'the Maiden', is Baal's sister and fiercest ally. In the Baal Cycle she shuts the doors of her house and makes war: she slays the people of seashore and sunrise, heads roll beneath her like balls, hands fly over her like locusts, and she ties heads to her back and hands to her belt. She wades knee-deep in the blood of soldiers, neck-deep in the gore of warriors, and her liver swells with laughter. Then she washes her hands in dew and rain.

When Baal is killed by Death, she searches for him in mourning, and at last seizes Mot, splits him with a sword, winnows him, burns him and scatters him in the fields.

In Egypt, where Anat and her companion Astarte were adopted in the New Kingdom, they appear as warrior goddesses on horseback and as consorts of the gods.
versions.caveat: Anat's sexual role is contested; the love side of the pairing is clearer in Astarte and Ishtar.

versions.title: Armed Aphrodite
versions.teaser: Aphrodite loved Ares, and at Sparta she carried weapons.
versions.text:
In Homer, Aphrodite is no warrior. When she enters the fighting at Troy to rescue her son Aeneas, Diomedes wounds her wrist, and Zeus gently tells her to stick to the works of marriage. Yet she is married to Hephaestus and in love with Ares, and the Odyssey's bard Demodocus sings how Hephaestus caught the two in bed in an invisible net, to the gods' 'unquenchable laughter'.

Her link to war was more than an affair. The traveller Pausanias saw at Sparta an ancient armed image of Aphrodite and a temple of Aphrodite Areia, 'warlike', and at Cythera, her sacred island, an armed image of Aphrodite Ourania. Scholars have long connected these with her likely Near Eastern ancestry in Astarte and Ishtar, goddesses who rode to battle.

In classical Greece the war side faded. It remained in the myth that love and war share a bed.
versions.caveat: Aphrodite's Near Eastern origin is widely accepted but debated, and armed Aphrodites were local cults, not her usual character.

image.file: File:Guillemot, Alexandre Charles - Mars and Venus Surprised by Vulcan - Google Art Project.jpg
image.caption: Mars and Venus Surprised by Vulcan, painting by Alexandre-Charles Guillemot, 1827

versions.title: Anāhitā, the Strong and Pure
versions.teaser: A river goddess whom heroes beseech for victory in battle.
versions.text:
Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā, 'the Moist, Strong, Undefiled', is the goddess of the heavenly river from which all waters flow. Her Avestan hymn, the Ābān Yašt, describes her as a tall, beautiful maiden in a golden mantle, wearing jewels, a crown of stars and a cloak of beaver skins, driving a chariot of four white horses: wind, rain, cloud and sleet.

She purifies men's seed and women's wombs and eases childbirth. Yet most of her hymn is a roll-call of kings and heroes, and even monsters, who sacrificed to her for victory. She grants it to Thraētaona against Aži Dahāka and to Kavi Haosrauuah against his rivals, and she refuses it to the wicked.

Under the Achaemenids Artaxerxes II set up her statues across the empire, and later Sasanian kings dedicated severed enemy heads in her temple at Istakhr.
versions.caveat: Anāhitā's martial side is as granter of victory rather than a fighter herself, and her likely Ishtar influence is debated.

versions.title: The Morrígan at the River
versions.teaser: The war goddess straddles a river and sleeps with the Dagda.
versions.text:
The Morrígan, 'Phantom Queen' or 'Great Queen', is the Irish goddess of war, prophecy and death, who often appears as a crow over the battlefield. In the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, before the great fight, the Dagda meets her at Samhain by the river Unshin in Connacht, washing herself with one foot on the south bank and one on the north. They sleep together, and the place is known ever after as 'the Bed of the Couple'. She then promises him victory and tells him where the enemy will land.

In the Táin Bó Cúailnge she appears to the hero Cú Chulainn as a beautiful woman offering him her love. When he rejects her, she attacks him in the ford as an eel, a wolf and a hornless heifer.

Her love is a pledge of victory, and a refusal is a declaration of war.

versions.title: Freyja Chooses the Slain
versions.teaser: The goddess of love takes half the battle dead to her hall.
versions.text:
Freyja is the most desired goddess in Norse myth: giants demand her as their price again and again, and Loki accuses her in Lokasenna of having slept with every god and elf in the hall. She weeps tears of red gold for her wandering husband Óðr and rides in a chariot drawn by cats.

She is also a goddess of the battle dead. The poem Grímnismál says that each day Freyja chooses half the fallen for her hall, Sessrúmnir, in the field of Fólkvangr, while Odin has the other half. Snorri adds that whenever she rides to battle, she takes half the slain. She also taught the Æsir seiðr, a sorcery that could be used to foresee and to shape fate.

The combination looks odd only from outside. A goddess of love who gathers the dead is claiming the whole of life at its most intense.

image.file: File:Freyja riding with her cats (1874).jpg
image.caption: Freyja riding in her cat-drawn wagon, illustration by Ludwig Pietsch
